hero.title: Light — Reflection & Refraction Made Crystal Clear
hero.hook: Why does a straw in water look bent? Why do you see your reflection in a still pond? Why do glasses correct vision? All of it comes down to two fundamental behaviors of light — reflection and refraction. These 7–8 marks in your boards explain everything from mirrors to telescopes to the human eye.

hook_section.scenario: Hold a spoon and look at the concave side — you see an inverted, magnified face. Turn it around and look at the convex side — right-side up, smaller. Same spoon, two curved surfaces, two completely different images. The difference? Curved mirrors form images in predictable ways based on where the object is placed relative to the focal point.
hook_section.bridge: Reflection (light bouncing off surfaces) and Refraction (light bending as it enters a new medium) are the two pillars of this chapter. Mirrors use reflection. Lenses use refraction. The mirror formula, lens formula, and magnification connect them mathematically.
hook_section.punchline: Mirror formula: 1/v + 1/u = 1/f. Lens formula: 1/v − 1/u = 1/f. Sign convention (New Cartesian): distances in direction of incident light are positive.

concept_section.analogy: Think of light rays as arrows fired at a surface. For reflection, angle in = angle out (like a billiard ball bounce). For refraction, the arrow bends as it crosses from one medium to another — like a person running from firm ground into water. They slow down and change direction at the boundary.
concept_section.principle: Snell's Law: n₁sin θ₁ = n₂sin θ₂. Refractive index n = speed of light in vacuum / speed in medium = c/v. Denser medium → slower speed → ray bends toward normal. Rarer medium → faster → ray bends away from normal.

reveals.question: 🔄 Concave mirror — image types?
reveals.answer: Object beyond C: real, inverted, diminished. At C: real, inverted, same size. Between C and F: real, inverted, magnified. At F: image at infinity. Between F and P: virtual, erect, magnified. Used in: torches, vehicles, shaving mirrors.

reveals.question: 🌐 Convex mirror — image types?
reveals.answer: Always virtual, erect, diminished — regardless of object position. Image always between P and F behind the mirror. Used in: rear-view mirrors, security mirrors — wider field of view.

reveals.question: 🔵 Convex lens — image types?
reveals.answer: Object beyond 2F: real, inverted, diminished. At 2F: real, inverted, same size. Between 2F and F: real, inverted, magnified. At F: image at infinity. Between F and O: virtual, erect, magnified. Used in: cameras, telescopes, eyes.

reveals.question: 🌈 Refraction effects?
reveals.answer: Apparent depth (objects in water look shallower): n = real depth / apparent depth. Total internal reflection: when angle of incidence exceeds critical angle in denser medium — basis of optical fibres, mirages, sparkling of diamonds.

points: Mirror formula: 1/f = 1/v + 1/u; focal length f = R/2 (R = radius of curvature)
Lens formula: 1/f = 1/v − 1/u; Power P = 1/f (in metres), unit = Dioptre (D)
Snell's Law: n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂; denser medium → ray bends toward normal
Total Internal Reflection: when light goes from dense to rare medium beyond critical angle

quiz.q: An object is placed at 2F from a convex lens. The image formed is:
quiz.exp: Object at 2F from convex lens: image forms at 2F on other side, real, inverted, and same size as object. Using lens formula: 1/v − 1/(−2f) = 1/f → v = 2f.

quiz.q: A concave mirror is used as a rear-view mirror. This statement is:
quiz.exp: Convex mirror is used as rear-view mirror because it always forms virtual, erect, diminished images and provides a wider field of view compared to plane or concave mirrors.

quiz.q: A lens has focal length −0.5m. Its power is:
quiz.exp: P = 1/f = 1/(−0.5) = −2D. Negative power means concave (diverging) lens. Negative focal length → diverging lens.

quiz.q: Light travels from glass (n=1.5) to air (n=1). At the critical angle, the refracted ray travels:
quiz.exp: At the critical angle, the refracted ray travels along the interface (90° to normal). Beyond this angle, total internal reflection occurs — no refracted ray, all light reflects back into glass.
